analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new offshore oil and gas drilling off the California, Oregon, and Washington coasts.
analysis.headline: The bill drew six Democratic cosponsors but never got a vote — it was referred to committee on the day it was introduced and sat there until the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write a permanent ban into federal law against leasing any part of the outer Continental Shelf off California, Oregon, or Washington for oil or gas exploration, development, or production. It was introduced in May 2010, in the weeks after the Deepwater Horizon rig explosion in the Gulf of Mexico. It died in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents and businesses in California, Oregon, and Washington — especially fishing fleets, tourism, and beach-dependent economies — gain protection from the risk of an offshore oil spill, which the 2010 Gulf disaster showed can shut down fisheries and beaches for months or years.
analysis.who_benefits_short: West Coast fishing and tourism communities

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act so that the Interior Secretary may not issue any lease for exploration, development, or production of oil or gas off California, Oregon, or Washington.
The ban is written into statute, which is harder for a future administration to reverse than the leasing plans and moratoria that had previously kept West Coast drilling off the table.
The prohibition covers the entire outer Continental Shelf off the three states, with no carve-outs for specific lease areas.

analysis.who_pays: The oil and gas industry gives up potential access to West Coast federal waters, and the federal treasury forgoes any future lease-sale bonuses and royalties from that area. Energy consumers could see marginally less domestic supply, though West Coast drilling was already effectively barred at the time.

drawbacks.text: A permanent statutory ban removes any flexibility to revisit West Coast drilling if safety technology improves or energy conditions change, locking today's policy into law.

The bill forgoes potential federal revenue from lease bonuses and royalties, and a small amount of potential domestic energy production, in an area where drilling was already effectively blocked by existing moratoria.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the communities on the Pacific coast, the protection from catastrophic spill risk outweighs the loss of revenue from drilling that was not happening anyway. The bill's weakness is design, not intent: a permanent, absolute ban is a blunt instrument compared with a periodically reviewed moratorium, and it hands its opponents a fair argument about flexibility and forgone federal revenue. On the substance, the tradeoff favors coastal protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and the 111th Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: Senator Barbara Boxer of California introduced the bill on May 13, 2010, with five Democratic colleagues — Cantwell, Feinstein, Merkley, Wyden, and Murray — joining as original cosponsors.
The introduction came weeks after the April 2010 Deepwater Horizon explosion in the Gulf of Mexico, which put offshore drilling risks in the national spotlight.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on May 13, 2010.
That referral was the last action ever taken; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed before the Congress ended in January 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The oil and gas industry came out ahead, since no statutory ban now stands in the way of any future administration proposing West Coast leases — though the West Coast remained off-limits under the separate leasing policies in place at the time. Coastal communities gained nothing from the bill's failure; they simply kept the pre-existing, less durable protections.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Senate Democrat; no Republican support is recorded anywhere in the bill's two-action history, and the bill never reached a vote that would have shown where the chamber stood.

industries.note: The bill permanently closes the federal waters off California, Oregon, and Washington to oil and gas leasing. The industry's interest in opening new areas runs against the coastal public's interest in avoiding spills, as the 2010 Gulf disaster demonstrated.

A spill off the West Coast would close fisheries and beaches and could take years to clean up; the bill removes that risk by statute. What protects the ocean also protects the region's fishing and tourism economies.
